extracted.intended_audience: academics, researchers, and administrators interested in how grant panels and peer review weigh interdisciplinarity and diversity
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive guidance and observed criteria used by grant panelists when evaluating academic research proposals, with emphasis on how interdisciplinarity and diversity are weighed alongside merit. Drawn from interviews and panel observations rather than prescriptive policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of intellectual world beyond narrow focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists value applicants' awareness of intellectual work outside their narrow specialty; lack of such awareness is considered a sign of narrowness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation: 'Awareness of the [intellectual] world beyond their focus . . . I consider it a sign of narrowness.' Anti-patterns include Eurocentric or Americano-centric sweeping statements that reveal ignorance or pomposity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of Eurocentrism / cultural myopia
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals (and scholars) should not make sweeping claims based solely on European/American frames; Eurocentrism/Americano-centrism is flagged as narrow and problematic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Panelists explicitly call out 'pomposity of people who make sweeping [statements] always . . . based on Europe' as a negative indicator when evaluating scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topical or geographic coverage that widens access to scarce materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers favor proposals that address topics or geographic areas which make available materials that are otherwise 'hard to find.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One sociologist favors proposals in his 'pet areas' not for personal reasons but because they 'make accessible materials that are otherwise hard to find.' This is treated as a positive evaluative factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Initial judgment on intrinsic scholarly quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Many panelists insist on grading proposals solely on perceived scholarly quality during their readings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: 'I prefer to grade on quality only.' This is often cited as the 'real evaluation' stage where meritocratic standards are applied without adjustment for representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of stages: quality scoring then representation-based adjustments
rubrics_metrics.description: Panelists often separate an initial 'real evaluation' (quality) from later deliberative ranking stages where representation or diversity may be factored in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as a conceptual framework that 'allows panelists to protect the sanctity of the process'—initial blind/quality-focused reading followed by shuffling/negotiated rankings to achieve representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of diversity/representation as a later balancing criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Diversity (geographic, disciplinary, institutional, demographic) is sometimes used after initial scoring to broaden who gets funded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a reviewer supported an archaeologist partly to 'widen the spectrum of people [whom] we funded'—but insists it wasn't simple tokenism; the proposal also made a substantive case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive, not tokenistic, justification for diversity-driven choices
rubrics_metrics.description: When diversity is invoked, reviewers prefer projects that have clear scholarly reasons for adding new perspectives rather than purely quota-based inclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the archaeology example where the project's focus (a particular spatial location) produced 'a very different understanding'—the reviewer valued its multi-dimensional scholarly payoff, not just increasing headcount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-dimensionality / interdisciplinary payoff
rubrics_metrics.description: Projects that integrate multiple perspectives or disciplines and thereby yield new, multi-dimensional understandings are valued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer praise: 'I liked the multi-dimensionality of the project'—valuing how interdisciplinary attention to space/cultural mixture can change understanding of a subject (e.g., medieval Islam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to factor affirmative action or diversification when lacking information
rubrics_metrics.description: Some panelists refuse to adjust evaluations for diversification/affirmative action either because they lack sufficient information or view it as ill-advised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted objection: 'There’s no way I will be able to figure that into my reading . . . I don’t have information [to make such judgments].' This stance leads to strictly quality-based scoring for those reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of institutional prestige and supervisor effects (elitism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers recognize that institutional prestige and famous advisers influence expectations and rankings—often seen as a bias toward elite institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An anthropologist observed: 'Those who have famous advisers and are at [the] top three or four universities will be ranked higher ... even if the quality of the proposal is the same.' This is noted as an endemic elitism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive fairness across institution types
rubrics_metrics.description: Some actors advocate spreading resources across types of institutions (e.g., four-year colleges, applied departments) to promote justice-inflected distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence from professional association politics (ASA vs APSA) shows attempts to make room for candidates from diverse institutional types; such distributive principles are a deliberate corrective to elitism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tension and complementarity between meritocracy and democratic/distributive aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluation often involves balancing meritocratic excellence with democratic/distributive fairness; reviewers conceptualize these as sometimes antinomic but frequently treated as additive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter concludes that 'excellence and diversity do not function as alternative criteria of evaluation, but as additive, complementary factors' and that diversity has become 'another manifestation of what is sacred in American academia.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Vulnerability of interdisciplinary and diversity-focused fields
rubrics_metrics.description: Interdisciplinary fields and those focused on marginalized populations (women’s studies, African-American studies, ethnic studies, cultural studies) risk being pushed to the periphery in evaluation processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes these fields 'struggle to keep from being pushed to the periphery' because older, established disciplines continue to 'define the rules of the game,' contributing to their fragility.
